Terminal-native agent multiplexer: surfaces the state of every coding agent at a glance — blocked, working, done — as real terminal panes rather than a wrapped interpretation of them. Self-described as "the runtime your coding agents live on."
Written in Rust; ships as a single binary rather than an Electron app, and runs inside whatever terminal is already in use.

Covers the multiplexer basics that make it a plausible tmux replacement rather than a companion: detach and reattach from any terminal, sessions that survive restarts, and attach over SSH. Weighed on Terminal/Multiplexer/Idea.
Keeps tmux-style prefix keys while treating mouse click, drag, and split as equally first-class, so neither input mode is the fallback.
Agent state detection is the premise: panes are labeled by whether the agent inside is blocked, working, or done, which is the piece a general-purpose multiplexer leaves to the human to infer.
A socket API lets agents drive the multiplexer themselves — spawning panes, reading output, and waiting on each other — rather than only being driven by a human at the prefix key.
Plugins extend panes and workflows, distributed through a marketplace.

Person/Chris Power switched over after about 10 years on tmux, won over by the agent-state pane and by being able to SSH into a remote box and leave an agent running unattended — Person/Chris Power/YouTube/26/08/herdr.
Installed from My/Dotfiles since as a global mise tool, alongside tmux rather than replacing it, to try the agent-state pane in daily use.

Config lives at ~/.config/herdr/config.toml and holds two settings. onboarding = false stops herdr's first-run write from editing a chezmoi-managed file; [update] version_check = false leaves the version to mise, which herdr already defers to. Its defaults supply the rest — the ctrl+b prefix and Catppuccin/Mocha.

Quit the editor the way that editor quits. The pane comes back by itself.
In Vim or Neovim, press Esc, then type :q and Enter. If it reports unsaved changes, type :q! and Enter instead.
:q! is safe here. The file is a copy, and herdr deletes it as soon as the editor exits. Discarding the changes loses nothing.
The pane you started from kept running the whole time. Nothing was waiting on you, and focus returns to that pane on its own.
The editor is whatever EDITOR names, so another setup may quit some other way. The section on which editor runs covers that.

prefix+e copies the focused pane's stored history into a temp file, then opens $EDITOR on that file in a second pane. The key name is keys.edit_scrollback, listed with its default in herdr's config reference.
herdr takes the copy once, at the moment of the keypress, and never updates it. While the editor is open the pane goes on printing into its own history, and the file stays as written.
Whatever you save in the editor stays in the copy. The pane keeps the history it had.

Reading a long pane history in an editor you already know. Copy mode offers literal search with / and ?, described in herdr's keyboard reference. An editor adds regular expressions, folding, marks, and split windows over the same text.
Getting text out of a pane that is awkward to select with the mouse. Once the history is a file, the editor's own copy and clipboard behaviour applies to all of it.

Reading everything the pane still holds in one go. The keypress asks for every retained row. herdr pane read --source recent-unwrapped runs the same read, described in herdr's CLI reference, but returns 80 rows by default and caps --lines at 1000 (src/app/api_helpers.rs:120-129). For a history longer than that, the keypress is the way to see all of it at once.
Working from the keyboard alone. The key acts on the focused pane, so there is no pane id to look up and no shell to run a command in.
Up to 1000 rows, both routes call the same function and return the same bytes (src/app/api_helpers.rs:120-129). The gain is the editor, so a script is better served by the command.
